a3631.speech: "The temporary suspension of exports of shea nuts is a decision that promotes the country's industrial development. This measure encourages local processors to increase their production capacity and to promote job creation all along the value chain. It makes it possible to retain a larger share of the wealth generated by this sector within the national economy." ; Explains that this resource is valued locally through the production of shea butter and press cake, and that her company's mission is to support the local economy by processing the nuts in Mali.

a3631.speaker: Kancou Keita Cissé, director of Mali-Shi
a3631.speech: "This suspension represents an opportunity to secure the supply of raw materials, because until now the plant has not managed to produce at full capacity." According to her, her company has a processing capacity of 30,000 tonnes of shea nuts per year, making it possible to produce about 12,000 tonnes of shea butter; she pledges to make the most of this opportunity by strengthening local partnerships.

a3631.speaker: Boubacar Sidiki Diabaté, secretary general of the National Federation of Oil and Animal Feed Producers of Mali
a3631.speech: Reports that the federation uses the entire seed production of the Malian Textile Development Company (CMDT) as well as imports from Brazil, amounting to some 350,000 tonnes. "The oil we produce does not cover the population's consumption needs. Every year we see that the market is flooded with oil coming from anywhere. During my trip to Brazil on behalf of my federation, I studied the possibilities of diversification in order to reproduce those models in Mali. In this period of insecurity, however, follow-up is complicated."

a3631.speaker: Boubacar Sidiki Diabaté, secretary general of the National Federation of Oil and Animal Feed Producers of Mali
a3631.speech: Stresses that his organisation produces between 40 and 50 million litres of oil per year. "The State has organised two workshops to encourage stakeholders to diversify their products. Some are currently testing soya, groundnut and even shea nuts. We need a structure to supervise these value chains, as the CMDT does for cotton seed," recalling that the export of cotton seed has been banned in Mali for more than a decade.

a3631.speaker: Soumaila Coulibaly, president of the sesame sector
a3631.speech: Says that this ban gives concrete form to a long-standing vision of agricultural stakeholders, focused on developing production, processing and marketing. "We have held discussions to preserve the gains of the sesame sector, particularly regarding price. With the price set at 600 CFA francs, we hope to maintain producers' interest." He insists on the importance of collaboration among the actors of the value chain, from production to storage, through to processing and marketing, in order to maximise the benefits for the country.

a3631.speaker: Abdoulaye Konaté, president of the Ouolofobougou market
a3631.speech: Believes that through this decision the authorities wish to promote local processing and guarantee an adequate supply to the factories; argues that certain varieties of groundnut, such as those intended for oil, should be processed locally, while others, such as fresh groundnuts, should be allowed to be exported. "Groundnuts support the livelihoods of thousands of people in Mali. We think the factories cannot absorb the entire production. Export is therefore essential, even for the State."

a3631.speaker: Zédion Dembélé, Director General of Trade, Consumer Affairs and Competition (DGCC)
a3631.speech: Explained at the signing of the suspension protocol that the main objective is to ensure the commitment of local units to buy the available stocks. "Once raw-material needs are covered, the surpluses may be exported." According to him, the measure will make cooking oil accessible to the population at affordable prices and on a continuous basis.

a3683.speaker: Taliban source (anonymous)
a3683.speech: Said the terrain was so rough in one part of the Mazar valley that one helicopter failed to land after three attempts.

a3683.speaker: Mir Zaman, earthquake survivor
a3683.speech: Told the BBC that he pulled his dead children out of the rubble by himself: “It was dark. There was no light. Someone lent me a lamp, and then I used a shovel and pick axe to dig them out. There was no one to help because everyone was affected. So many people died in my village. Some are still buried. Whole families have died,” he said.

a3683.speaker: Khawat Gul, uncle of injured child Maiwand
a3683.speech: “You can see his situation. It's so tragic. The earthquake was deadly. I want the doctors to treat him, to cure him,” said the child's uncle.

a3683.speaker: Nader Khan, earthquake survivor at Jalalabad's Nangrahar Regional Hospital
a3683.speech: Recalled how he lost two sons and two daughters-in-law to the earthquake and said he was able to save two grandchildren but now does not know where they are: “I injured my head and spine, so I couldn't move to save them... I don't know what has happened to the bodies of my sons,” he told the BBC.

a3683.speaker: United Nations
a3683.speech: Calls the situation in Afghanistan an unprecedented crisis of hunger; has released emergency funds.

a3683.speaker: David Lammy, Britain's Foreign Secretary
a3683.speech: Said aid from the UK will be “channelled through experienced partners”, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) and the International Red Cross.

a3683.speaker: Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, Indian Foreign Minister
a3683.speech: Wrote on X after speaking to his Taliban counterpart Amir Khan Muttaqi that India delivered 1,000 tents to Kabul; said the Indian mission is also helping to move 15 tonnes of food from Kabul to Kunar province, which has been badly hit by the earthquake, adding that India would send more relief items.

a3683.speaker: Amy Martin, head of the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in Afghanistan
a3683.speech: Said survivors will need housing, shelter and blankets.

a3948.speaker: Namibian Broadcasting Corporation (NBC) and Namibia Press Agency (NAMPA)
a3948.speech: Have reaffirmed their longstanding partnership, committing to deepen cooperation in content sharing, resource utilisation and newsroom collaboration.

a3948.speaker: Telecom Namibia
a3948.speech: Has warned that the escalating copper theft is threatening critical telecommunications infrastructure and putting lives at risk, calling for stronger law enforcement and government intervention.

a3948.speaker: Lucia Iipumbu, Namibian Minister of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security
a3948.speech: Revealed during a Cabinet Committee Briefing on Friday that Namibia’s visa-on-arrival system has generated more than N$413 million in revenue in less than 12 months.

a3948.speaker: Organisers of Namibia’s 36th Independence Day celebrations in the Kunene Region
a3948.speech: Expressed confidence that the town of Khorixas is ready to host the regional event scheduled for March 21, 2026.

a3948.speaker: Yarukeekuro Steven Ndorokaze, NamRA Chief of Strategic Communications, Stakeholder Engagement, and Taxpayer Education
a3948.speech: Described the N$90 billion owed to the Namibia Revenue Agency by taxpayers as a historic debt.

a3948.speaker: Pan African Women’s Organisation (PAWO)
a3948.speech: Has strongly condemned the United States government’s latest sanctions against Cuba, describing it as a deliberate attempt to destabilise Cuba.

a3964.speaker: Yusef Taylor, spokesperson for Team Gom Sa Bopa
a3964.speech: "PURA's decision is a betrayal of the Gambian people," said moments before his arrest. "This price floor protects telecom profits while pricing out low-income citizens, stifling digital innovation, and restricting access to education and jobs."

a3964.speaker: Coalition of civil society organizations (EFSCRJ, GALA and Team Gom Sa Bopa) (joint statement and petition)
a3964.speech: Condemned PURA's new policy as "anti-competitive" and a direct assault on affordable internet access ; the petition outlined their demands for the immediate suspension of the price floor, full transparency on the cost model and benchmarks used to justify the policy, and the implementation of a price ceiling to protect consumers, and called for tangible improvements in internet service quality ; emphasized that PURA's mandate, under Section 13 of the PURA Act, is to protect consumers and enforce service standards, not to shield telecom companies from competition ; "The price floor is a regressive step that burdens ordinary Gambians. If PURA were truly committed to the public interest, it would impose a price ceiling and demand better service quality, not raise costs to protect GSM operators." ; issued an ultimatum to PURA, demanding the suspension of the price floor by the close of business on Wednesday, August 27, 2025, and vowed to escalate their campaign if their demands are not met.

a3964.speaker: Madi Jobarteh, Executive Director of the Edward Francis Small Centre for Rights and Justice (EFSCRJ)
a3964.speech: "This was a peaceful protest, and the heavy-handed response from the police is unacceptable. The right to protest is enshrined in our constitution, and PURA must answer for this policy that punishes the most vulnerable."

a3964.speaker: Gambia Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (GCCPC)
a3964.speech: Has publicly opposed the price floor, arguing that recent tariff competition had benefited small businesses and low-income households.

a3964.speaker: Witnesses to the protest
a3964.speech: Described the arrests as chaotic, with police detaining individuals seemingly at random.

a3964.speaker: Fatou Jagne, university student who attended the protest
a3964.speech: "This isn't just about data; it's about access to opportunity. How can we compete in a global economy when the cost of being online is out of reach for so many?"

a3964.speaker: Social media user (anonymous)
a3964.speech: "This is a fight for our future. We won't be silenced."

a3964.speaker: Gambian authorities (non-response)
a3964.speech: Authorities have yet to comment on the arrests or the status of the detainees.

a4032.speaker: European Union
a4032.speech: Has lauded Governor Babagana Umara Zulum's post-conflict recovery efforts, citing the Muna Vocational Training Institute, which trains youth, particularly those affected by the over one-decade-long Boko Haram insurgency.

a4032.speaker: Gautier Mignot, Ambassador, Head of the European Union mission to Borno
a4032.speech: Noted his team was delighted to see the magnitude of opportunity the vocational enterprise institute provides for the people of Borno State and beyond. He said, "I'm applauding this wonderful achievement. It's one example of many centres built by the state government under the guidance of Governor Zulum and his vision." ; "Vocational training is clear- it is something that young people in the state need, and this is something we have also experienced in Europe, especially in Germany." ; "We've been reviewing the portfolio of projects and humanitarian assistance and, above all, developing cooperation in many areas. Borno State has been and will remain a key priority area for European cooperation in the coming years."

a4032.speaker: Karen Jensen, representative of the German Ambassador
a4032.speech: Commended Governor Zulum for an all-inclusive empowerment which comprises women and girls; expressed satisfaction over the number of women participating in various vocational training programs at the facility, notably in traditionally male-dominated fields like welding, saying, "It's important for women and girls to be part of vocational education." ; "I'm proud of what I'm seeing here and our cooperation work is very nice."

a4032.speaker: European Union (delegation at the Government House courtesy call)
a4032.speech: Reiterated its commitment to partner with the Borno State Government in peace-building projects to be implemented by the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ).

a4032.speaker: Koffy Dominique Kouacou, representative of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Nigeria and ECOWAS
a4032.speech: Commended Governor Zulum's leadership qualities in promoting agriculture and strengthening local economies through innovation, infrastructure development, and capacity building. He stated they will work with the Zulum administration to determine the most effective ways to support the state government's efforts by enhancing agricultural productivity, establishing sustainable and resilient food systems, and empowering farmers and communities to become self-reliant.

a4181.speaker: Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, Djibouti's Minister of National Education and Vocational Training
a4181.speech: Welcomed the American delegation and immediately stressed his complete satisfaction with the very efficient framework of cooperation between USAID and MENFOP: “We wish to see cooperation with USAID and the other partners strengthened in order to help improve the employability of young people.”

a4181.speaker: Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, Djibouti's Minister of National Education and Vocational Training
a4181.speech: Then gave an overview of the state of Djiboutian schooling, ranging widely over the various ongoing projects with USAID and the other partners aimed at strengthening the quality of teaching and learning, and mentioned the new strategy put in place by the government under technical and vocational education and training (ETFP), which is a major lever for fighting unemployment and precarity.

a4181.speaker: Sean Jones, USAID Mission Director for the region
a4181.speech: Assured the minister that cooperation between USAID and the Djiboutian government would continue and be strengthened, and emphasised the American public aid agency's complete availability and total support for the education sector: “We will continue to invest in the education sector and therefore in the future of Djiboutian youth,” he declared, before adding that “American partnership and investments will cover the path of young Djiboutians from primary school through to university or vocational training, in order to help them meet the requirements of employability and enter the labour market.”

a4245.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) analysis, “Trends in Official Development Assistance and Implications on Social Sector Financing for Children”
a4245.speech: Says that beyond 2027, most donors are already signalling a reduction in their funding to Malawi, which will put a further strain on the sustainability of social sector spending; argues that the reduction comes at a time Malawi is reeling from an already fragile economic position with limited fiscal safeguards to mitigate the impact due to weak revenue collection and escalating debt-servicing costs ; “The reduction in ODA to Malawi threatens to exacerbate the country's existing macroeconomic vulnerabilities and derail its long-term development trajectory” ; “For many Malawians, the long-term impact of these funding cuts will be profoundly felt across key sectors such as health, education, food security and economic development, unless the gaps are adequately filled.”

a4245.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a4245.speech: Warns that without alternative financing, the sustained decline in donor funding will not only strain public budgets, but also exacerbate poverty and inequality, suppressing long-term economic growth.

a4245.speaker: United Nations (published data cited)
a4245.speech: Published data show that between 2017 and 2023, ODA remained the largest inflow, averaging $1.6 billion (about K2.8 trillion) compared with FDI averaging $144 million (about K252 billion) and remittances at an average of $219 million (K383 billion); in relative terms ODA flows to Malawi constituted 82 percent of total external inflows in 2023, compared to FDI at 10 percent and remittances at eight percent, according to the UN.

a4245.speaker: Bertha Bangara-Chikadza, President, Economics Association of Malawi
a4245.speech: Observed in an interview on Friday that the dwindling ODA has a number of implications for Malawi, as grants by donor countries or international organisations to support development projects have played a vital role in addressing the country's socio-economic challenges such as health, education and infrastructure ; “This means a decrease in ODA grants impact the delivery of essential services and hinder poverty reduction efforts.”

a4245.speaker: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
a4245.speech: Earlier warned that least developed countries are experiencing declines in aid flows, with data showing that their share of global ODA decreased to 22 percent in 2022, the lowest in over a decade.

a4245.speaker: United Nations
a4245.speech: According to the UN, aid is also being increasingly provided through concessional loans rather than grants, increasing developing countries' debt burdens at a time of growing debt distress.

a4245.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs of Malawi
a4245.speech: Projected that the financing of the national budget through tax revenues will increase to 53.6 percent in 2025/26 as grant financing will reduce to 14.2 percent.

a4304.speaker: Ambassadors of 105 countries to the United Nations in New York, including Mozambique (joint letter of 10 October)
a4304.speech: Signed a letter expressing their “profound concern” at the recent statements by Israel’s minister of foreign affairs declaring Secretary-General António Guterres persona non grata; condemned them and consider that such statements and other actions may undermine the capacity of the United Nations to carry out its mandate, which includes mediation in conflicts and the provision of humanitarian aid; hold that Israel’s actions can only contribute to delaying the end of hostilities in the Middle East and efforts to establish a roadmap leading to the two-State solution ; “In moments of heightened tension, the role of the Secretary-General is essential for the promotion of dialogue and understanding between parties in conflict” ; “We are confident of his commitment to peace and security, and alignment with International Law, including in promoting respect for international humanitarian law and the relevant United Nations resolutions on the situation in the Middle East” ; “constructive engagement with the United Nations is vital for overcoming the challenges we face and achieving a future of peace.”

a4304.speaker: Minister of Foreign Affairs of Israel
a4304.speech: Made recent statements declaring the Secretary-General of the United Nations, António Guterres, persona non grata.

a4457.speaker: Group of young African leaders at the Mandela Washington Fellows gathering (Accra, Kigali and Johannesburg, 2019)
a4457.speech: One consensus emerged: Africa's education systems must undergo urgent reforms to prepare students for the demands of the 21st century, meaning curriculum reforms, training super-teachers, and equipping students with critical thinking skills.

a4536.speaker: António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a4536.speech: Warned before the Security Council that the Sudanese people are caught in a “nightmare of violence, hunger, disease and displacement” ; “The suffering is increasing day by day, with nearly 25 million people in need of humanitarian assistance”, describing the disastrous conditions facing civilians 18 months after the start of the conflict ; stressed that “thousands of civilians” have been killed while countless others suffer “unspeakable violence”, notably widespread rape and sexual assault ; warned that violence and massacres, particularly in Aj Jazirah State, threaten to destabilise the entire region, from the Sahel to the Red Sea ; added that since last April more than 11 million people have fled, three million of them to neighbouring countries.

a4536.speaker: António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a4536.speech: Issued a fresh appeal to the SAF and the RSF to end hostilities and favour a negotiated solution: “Instead of easing tensions, they are intensifying military action”, he deplored, also denouncing the involvement of outside powers that are “pouring fuel on the fire.”

a4536.speaker: António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a4536.speech: Set out three priorities for protecting civilians: an immediate cessation of hostilities, strengthened measures for the protection of civilians, and the prosecution of those responsible for war crimes; considering that the “conditions are not met” for deploying a UN protection force in Sudan, he affirmed that the Secretariat remains ready to engage in discussions with the Security Council and other actors to explore concrete solutions to reduce violence and protect civilian populations.

a4678.speaker: Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, Zimbabwe Health and Child Care Minister
a4678.speech: Has said Zimbabwe has sufficient stocks of HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria medicines, and additional supplies are being purchased; said that while the withdrawal of funding for these via USAID by the United States in January caught the government off guard, authorities quickly moved in to cover the gap ; “So we have enough stocks up to the end of June. But the stocks which were meant to cover the period from the end of June to the end of November have been halted. We cannot predict what will happen after the 90 days, but we expect to refuel the entire program.”

a4678.speaker: Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, Zimbabwe Health and Child Care Minister
a4678.speech: “In terms of service delivery, for those on HIV, TB, and malaria treatment, there will be no disruption. No one should change the way they are taking their medicine.”

a4678.speaker: Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, Zimbabwe Health and Child Care Minister
a4678.speech: Said the government had already floated a tender to purchase more medical supplies that will cover the June-September period ; “The challenges that remain are related to procurement. We had medicines for HIV, TB, and malaria that had been procured, but these came in phases” ; “Now, what we have done as a government is to mobilize the necessary resources. And I think today, some of you may have seen in the papers that we have actually floated a tender for procurement of medicines. This will cover us from June to the end of September, depending on how other resources are managed.”

a4678.speaker: Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, Zimbabwe Health and Child Care Minister
a4678.speech: Explained that the funding gap caused by the major donor pullout was significant: “Let me start by saying the executive order from the President of the United States came as a surprise in January. We had workers at the primary healthcare level and our village healthcare workers, almost 19,000 of them, who were being paid by our partners. We also had over 8,000 nurses, some of whom were not in our opportunistic infection clinics. Most of these workers were involved in HIV, AIDS, TB, and malaria programs, so these are the programs that have been mainly affected by the executive order.”

a4678.speaker: Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, Zimbabwe Health and Child Care Minister
a4678.speech: Noted that the government moved quickly to address the situation: “This disruption only lasted a few days, and we stepped in to deploy our nurses to fill the gap. There were also a number of doctors and people working in laboratory services and administration. But we ensured that services were not disrupted by the absence of relief workers” ; mentioned that a 90-day waiver from the USA provided temporary relief: “So the nurses who were involved in the treatment clinics were ordered to return to work, and they are back on duty. Doctors are also working in hospitals, not just doing administrative work, but actively treating patients.”

a4728.speaker: Kadiri Edah, Director of the FCT Pilgrims Welfare Board
a4728.speech: Assured that the FCT Administration would continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of pilgrims by maintaining high standards of facilities both here and abroad.

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC)
a4908.speech: Though quite aware that President Lazarus Chakwera’s followers will dismiss the concerns PAC raised during a meeting with the Malawi Congress Party (MCP) leader, they maintained that the doubt is loud and clear on him to be voted back into office even in his strongholds of the Central Region.

a4908.speaker: Monsignor Dr. Patrick Thawale, PAC chairperson
a4908.speech: Said they were aware that after raising the issues they brought with them, “your people will engage you to dismiss what we have raised”. “The question they ought to answer is whether after raising national issues with you on 28th November, 2023, service delivery and economy have improved” ; “Although road construction is excellent, for us the standard of living has gone down; the perception that the regime is corrupt still stands; that most civil servants are frustrated remains a fact; and that fuel crisis continues is a reality” ; “As regards your leadership, the observation is that action-oriented leadership has lacked. The general view is that there has been failed leadership tainted with hypocrisy” ; “There are strong observations that by failing to act on officials allegedly involved in corrupt practices, your leadership may be benefitting from the civil service leadership and those Ministers named in such corrupt acts” ; “The general political atmosphere puts your political party on the exit stage unless something spectacular emerges. Even in your strongholds, the doubt on your winning is loud and clear. It is our hope that in the remaining months you can always turn around this perception” ; “The doubt is real. The failures are massive and obvious. We are calling upon you to act on issues of national importance before the public rises against you. Patience has limits.”

a4908.speaker: Monsignor Dr. Patrick Thawale, PAC chairperson
a4908.speech: Assured that the observations made were “honest and frank”: “It is true that a real friend should always offer constructive criticism... Given that your faith in the word of God is as strong as ever, we also believe that ‘Wounds from a sincere friend are better than many kisses from an enemy’ (Proverbs 27:6).”

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC)
a4908.speech: Focused on corruption, economy, governance aspects and civil service gaps, saying: “It is our view that these are so intertwined that one cannot separate them. In no way we wish to advocate for any candidate in the 2025 elections as we raise the issues. We approach Your Excellency as father of the nation.”

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC)
a4908.speech: On corruption: maintained that the Chakwera-led administration is inactive and indecisive on several revelations of alleged corrupt practices in the higher echelons of his government. “Your administration has demonstrated serious weaknesses on the alleged abuse of funds and corruption despite your assertions made during 2019 and 2020 campaign” ; “We wish to recall that as a Man of God you exuded immense hope to take a strong stand against corrupt practices” ; “Indeed, the country’s socio-economic, financial, human, and political environment has been corruptly destroyed... incidents bent on corrupt practices in the current administration have been rife in the areas of AIP, and fuel procurement” ; “The inaction and indecisiveness in many fronts of government not only manifest lack of statecraft but also cluelessness on operations of state machinery” ; “Words have not matched your actions on issues of corruption and alleged abuse of funds in the administration.”

a4908.speaker: MCP Manifesto (document)
a4908.speech: States: ‘The MCP will be very tough on corruption because it realises that corruption is an epidemic that has the power to completely destroy a country’s socio-economic, financial and human and political environment’ (p.17) ; ‘In fighting corruption, therefore, the MCP’s capable democratic developmental state will not only take steps to increase incomes but also to improve the people’s standard of living’ (p.18) ; ‘The ultimate goal of the MCP will be to establish a public sector that maximises public value... An MCP government will bring to an end the current situation whereby a career of work for the state turns into the reserved privilege of the few while maladministration and ineffectiveness are encouraged’ (p.16).

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC)
a4908.speech: On the economy: observed that the economy is in bad shape. “Your Excellency, currently the standard of living in Malawi is disastrous. Prices of basic commodities do no match the income your followers earn. It is talk of the town on your failure to manage the economy” ; welcomed the appointment of the new Reserve Bank Governor and requested that he be given the necessary support ; “There are negative observations on your number of international trips and those of your Cabinet Ministers” ; “Although, we share the view that the world economy faces challenges, we believe you have not lived to public expectation as demonstrated by a voice of cry from the masses, rendering your austerity measures futile.”

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC)
a4908.speech: On civil service leadership gaps: told the President that when they last met they “kindly impressed” on him to motivate the civil service by acting on critical issues affecting it. “Clearly, Your Excellency, you may have ignored advice that may have contributed positively to service delivery” ; “the Office of the President & Cabinet is said to be dysfunctional and demotivating the Civil Service, let alone the entire public service” ; “Your Excellency may wish to be reminded that the critical position of Principal Secretary Administration in OPC has been vacant since 2022 — kindly reconfigure the higher echelons of administration.”

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC)
a4908.speech: On the 2025 elections and conflict prevention: “Electoral processes can build or destroy a country if not properly handled” ; “we appreciate your condemnation of violence in various remarks made by your office. However, it is disappointing to note that it is alleged that MCP is becoming another instrument for oppression as we move to 2025 Elections. The action to stifle demonstration organised by the opposition was primitive act in the democratic Malawi. So too, we do not condone stoning of Presidential motorcades” ; “We observe that several arrests of prominent figures have been effected recently... we urge your government to ensure that these acts are not aimed at victimising those who hold opposing views” ; “We are not against the rule of law. We believe in it.”

a4908.speaker: Public Affairs Committee (PAC) leadership
a4908.speech: In its preamble, expressed appreciation that the Capital City’s road network “has been transformed”, adding that “the quality of the road construction we witness today is amazing” ; “For some time we have been waiting for such type of road infrastructure — Lilongwe has become a source of pride. This is excellent work” ; expressed appreciation over Chakwera’s “tolerance even in most difficult times” ; “We may safely state it is God’s intervention for you to assume office... Coming from our fraternity, we are proud of you” ; observed that international relations between Malawi and other countries have improved.

a4972.speaker: Government of Zimbabwe
a4972.speech: Has commended Old Mutual for equipping youths with core competencies needed in the modern world through its Schools Quiz competition.

a4972.speaker: Professor Mavima, Minister of Skills Audit and Development
a4972.speech: Speaking at the 42nd anniversary celebrations of the quiz competition, said the quiz was more than a contest of knowledge as it was a crucible of mental agility and strategic intellect: "This is not just a commemoration of years gone by; it is a celebration of legacy, of progress, and of the limitless potential ignited in Zimbabwean youngsters through the power of knowledge" ; applauded the initiative for nurturing vital skills such as adaptability, communication, and critical thinking, which are essential not only in academic settings but also across various sectors of the economy: "These are not just quiz skills; they are employability skills, leadership skills, and life skills."

a4972.speaker: Professor Mavima, Minister of Skills Audit and Development
a4972.speech: Praised the quiz for being inclusive, offering equal opportunities for learners from diverse backgrounds: "Talent knows no boundary and gender. This competition provides a level playing field where rural and urban, privileged and underprivileged, boys and girls, all gather on one platform" ; also commended the organisers for preserving national identity and cultural heritage through the event, highlighting how the quiz serves as an anchor for young people amid an increasingly digital and globalised world.

a4972.speaker: Professor Mavima, Minister of Skills Audit and Development
a4972.speech: Congratulating the winners, urged them to "walk into the future with confidence, curiosity, and a deep sense of national pride," adding that many of today's leaders trace their first sparks of ambition to moments like these.

a4993.speaker: Duma Boko, President of Botswana and Chairman of the African Leaders Malaria Alliance (ALMA)
a4993.speech: Said the continent needs an additional $5.2 billion per year to fight malaria, and released a statement that noted that although Botswana and Tanzania are great examples of countries progressing well in the fight against malaria, the continent at large needs financial assistance to arrest the increase in infections; he implored African governments to prioritise malaria in their national budgets: "Governments must prioritise malaria in national budgets and mobilise domestic private sector resources. Innovation must be made accessible swiftly, cutting procurement delays and fast-tracking approvals for life-saving tools. We are dangerously off track to meet the African Union's target to eliminate malaria by 2030, with cases rising once again. This crisis is worsened by funding cuts from key donors. In 2023, reductions in US foreign aid, historically a cornerstone of malaria elimination through the President's Malaria Initiative and the Global Fund, have disrupted programmes, causing dangerous stockouts of essential malaria commodities." ; "Without urgent course correction, Africa could face 112 million additional malaria cases and up to 280,000 more deaths over the 2027-2029 period. A low Global Fund replenishment could make the situation even graver. But there is hope. Countries are deploying new tools, including dual-insecticide nets, seasonal chemoprevention and the rollout of malaria vaccines. Community health workers, often the first line of defence, are saving lives daily. Strengthening their support and integrating malaria into broader health services, including antenatal care and school programmes, is vital."

a5429.speaker: Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State
a5429.speech: Has said an exception to the spending freeze allows emergency food assistance to continue.

a5429.speaker: Marcia Wong, former senior USAID official briefed on the situation
a5429.speech: Said about 500,000 metric tons of food worth $340 million is in limbo, in transit or storage, as humanitarian organizations wait for U.S. State Department approval to distribute it.

a5429.speaker: Aid workers (anonymous)
a5429.speech: Told Reuters that U.S.-provided cash assistance intended to help people buy food and other necessities in Sudan and Gaza also has been halted, as has funding for volunteer-run community kitchens, an American-supported effort in Sudan to help feed people in areas inaccessible to traditional aid.

a5429.speaker: At least six sources (anonymous)
a5429.speech: Said questions about what programs have permission to continue have gone unanswered, because the people who normally field such inquiries – officials at USAID – have been placed on leave.

a5429.speaker: Mark Moore, chief executive officer of Mana Nutrition of Georgia
a5429.speech: “We are the one thing that nearly everyone agrees on – that little children who are starving and need emergency aid need help.” ; “It is not hype or conjecture or hand wringing or even contested use of stats to say that hundreds of thousands of malnourished children could die without USAID.”

a5429.speaker: U.S. government
a5429.speech: Notified Mana and the other manufacturer, Edesia Nutrition of Rhode Island, that the stop-work orders had been rescinded.

a5429.speaker: U.S. State Department
a5429.speech: Did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

a5429.speaker: 2024 Global Report on Food Crises
a5429.speech: According to the report, in 2023 almost 282 million people in 59 countries and territories experienced extreme food shortages that threatened their lives or livelihoods.

a5429.speaker: Two aid workers in Sudan (anonymous)
a5429.speech: Said almost 30,000 metric tons of food meant to feed acutely malnourished children and adults in famine-stricken Sudan is in limbo, some sitting in hot warehouses where it is in danger of spoiling ; one of the workers said the food includes lentils, rice and wheat – enough to feed at least 2 million people for a month – and that some items have a quick expiration date and will be inedible by the end of Trump’s 90-day pause.

a5429.speaker: Researchers who collect and analyze data on food insecurity and famine
a5429.speech: Say FEWS NET is essential to world efforts to fight hunger, that it can be more nimble and prolific than its U.N.-backed counterpart, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification system (IPC), and that because FEWS NET doesn’t face the IPC’s consensus-building requirements it is faster and more efficient.

a5429.speaker: Recent Reuters investigation
a5429.speech: Found that the IPC’s requirement of consensus among local government authorities and representatives of other humanitarian bodies can result in political attempts to influence its work and can delay and impede its efforts to alert the world to a looming crisis.

a5429.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)
a5429.speech: Declined to comment on FEWS NET’s demise.

a5429.speaker: Frank Nyakairu, spokesman for IPC
a5429.speech: Said the “implications for the initiative remain unclear.”

a5429.speaker: Andrew Natsios, professor at Texas A&M University who headed USAID from 2001 to 2006
a5429.speech: “Ending FEWS NET is sort of like taking the steering wheel off the car. Even if the car is working fine, if there’s no steering wheel, you don’t know where the car is going.”

a5429.speaker: Alex de Waal, executive director of the World Peace Foundation at Tufts University’s Fletcher School
a5429.speech: Said that without FEWS NET, “the single most important component of the IPC system is knocked out.”

a5429.speaker: Reuters (December report)
a5429.speech: Reported in December that the Sudanese government maneuvered to delay an IPC famine determination in Darfur.

a5429.speaker: Jack Lew, U.S. ambassador to Israel from October 2023 until January
a5429.speech: Wrote that it was “irresponsible” to issue a FEWS NET finding projecting famine by early 2025 in part of northern Gaza.

a5429.speaker: FEWS NET
a5429.speech: Withdrew the report on northern Gaza, stating that its alert was “under further review” and that it expected to update the report in January.

a5429.speaker: FEWS NET employees
a5429.speech: Say they are not optimistic about the organization resuming work, with the dissolution of its chief funder, USAID.

a5429.speaker: Chris Newton, analyst specializing in early warning and food security at International Crisis Group
a5429.speech: Said FEWS NET’s apparent death leaves “a gaping hole” in reporting on humanitarian crises, and that its loss will hurt efforts to end famine in Sudan and prevent it in other hotspots and could lead to the collapse of a wide network of data providers, all crucial to understanding humanitarian risks globally ; “Famine was disappearing from the world in the 2000s, and now its return will likely accelerate as we become increasingly blind to it, even as it becomes a more common tool of politics and war.”

a5460.speaker: Port Autonome d'Abidjan (PAA) website
a5460.speech: A delegation of the Groupe Lithium Mali is on a strategic visit to the Port Autonome d'Abidjan (PAA), as can be read on the Port Autonome d'Abidjan's website, this Thursday 9 January 2025.

a5460.speaker: Myriam Ouassenan, Managing Director of the Abidjan Bulk Terminal (head of the delegation)
a5460.speech: Confirmed the intention of GOULAMINA LOGISTIQUE, the operational entity of LM SA, to use the Port of Abidjan as a strategic platform for the export of minerals, in particular those from the Goulamina project.

a5460.speaker: Berte Ibrahima, Manager of GOULAMINA LOGISTIQUE
a5460.speech: Presented the group's ambitions and requested the support of the Ivorian port authorities in order to ensure the imminent start of export operations via the bulk terminal.

a5460.speaker: Hien Yacouba Sie, Managing Director of the Port Autonome d'Abidjan
a5460.speech: While welcoming this initiative, reaffirmed the Port of Abidjan's capacity to respond effectively to these needs; stressed that the port's modern and secure infrastructure will facilitate trade flows, thereby strengthening economic ties between Mali and Cote d'Ivoire.

a5559.speaker: Thembinkosi Dube, local economist
a5559.speech: Says the 90-day pause on the 10 per cent import tariff is not a sigh of relief as anything can still happen, referring to the similar situation of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) where the American president paused the aid for 90 days, however, later on implemented the complete halt of the aid in several countries: "I do not think anything can stop him from finally implementing the tariffs, so it is a wait and see situation and it is almost certain that he might stick to his decision." ; stated that Trump had created a resilient mode for countries, as they were now creating other ways on how they can trade.

a5559.speaker: Thembinkosi Dube, local economist
a5559.speech: Highlighted the performance of the lilangeni amid ongoing global trade tensions, noting a drastic decline against the USD: "As of yesterday, the exchange rate was over E19." ; warned that if the global trade wars continued, the situation could worsen for the lilangeni: "We have observed that the lilangeni is weakening; yesterday it closed at E19.5 to the USD and E25 to the pound sterling, which is unprecedented." ; explained that the currency's value was heavily influenced by demand, and with the tariffs affecting South African commodities, demand has declined, further impacting the lilangeni's value: "If tensions between the two countries persist, we might find ourselves in a situation where the lilangeni weakens further, potentially beyond E20. If the situation continues, I believe that by next week we could be above E20."

a5559.speaker: Thembinkosi Dube, local economist
a5559.speech: Cautioned that if brent crude prices could rise again next week, the ministry of natural resources might announce an increase in fuel prices, which would contribute to inflation.

a5559.speaker: Thembinkosi Dube, local economist
a5559.speech: Stated that these trade wars could not continue indefinitely: "At some point, it will hit a peak and bring about a lasting solution. What is happening is that President Trump is pushing his own agenda while also solidifying the need for BRICS, where countries could potentially move away from the dollar. Once that happens, it could be irreversible."

a5559.speaker: The White House
a5559.speech: Deemed goods from approximately 60 trade partners, including the European Union and China, as coming from the 'worst offenders', which faced significantly higher rates.

a5559.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5559.speech: Framed these increased tariffs as retaliation for perceived unfair trade policies.

a5559.speaker: Analysts
a5559.speech: Predicting higher prices for American consumers and a slowdown in US economic growth.

a5908.speaker: Abdourahamane Tiani, President of the Republic of Niger, Head of State (Army General)
a5908.speech: Ordered a series of measures, including the sale of grey cement at a reduced price, to facilitate the reconstruction of homes destroyed by the 2024 floods.

a5908.speaker: Mahamadou Ibrahim Bagadoma, Governor of the Diffa region (Major General)
a5908.speech: In officially launching the operation, noted that an average reduction of 35% has been applied to the usual prices, which ranged between 85,000 and 100,000 FCFA per tonne depending on the region, and announced that in the Diffa region the price of a tonne of cement has been set at 59,000 FCFA; he then reported that Diffa has received 50 trucks, i.e. 2,225 tonnes of 32.5 grey cement, distributed as 33 trucks for the commune of Diffa and its surroundings, 7 for Maïné Soroa, 4 for Goudoumaria, 2 for Ngourti, 2 for Bosso and 2 for Nguigmi.

a5908.speaker: Mahamadou Ibrahim Bagadoma, Governor of the Diffa region (Major General)
a5908.speech: Expressed his gratitude to the Minister of Trade and Industry and to the Government for their constant efforts to improve the living conditions of the population, and praised the support of the cement companies MCC and MBM and of local economic operators, notably Mr Charfo Aboubacar.

a5908.speaker: Mahamadou Ibrahim Bagadoma, Governor of the Diffa region (Major General)
a5908.speech: Issued an appeal for strict respect of the official price and warned against any attempt at speculative resale of the cement.

a6047.speaker: MCA-Lesotho (Millennium Challenge Account – Lesotho II), notice to contractors
a6047.speech: “This serves to inform you that MCA-Lesotho II has received guidance from MCC on the final determination regarding the future of the Compact. Regrettably, the determination is that the Lesotho Health and Horticulture Compact will be closing. We do not have any guidance at this stage on how the closure process will unfold and await further instructions in the coming days” ; the notice further indicated that contractor services would remain in place until MCA-Lesotho confirms a definitive closure date.

a6047.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), during the Joe Biden administration
a6047.speech: Had lauded Lesotho for the successful launch of Compact II, describing it as a transformative investment in health and agriculture with the potential to uplift lives.

a6047.speaker: Palesa Motleleng, MCA-Lesotho Communications Officer
a6047.speech: When contacted for comment, declined to definitively confirm the Compact's closure, saying a press conference was being planned to formally announce its status.

a6047.speaker: Keneuoe Mojaki, spokesperson for the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning
a6047.speech: Said a press briefing would soon be held to address the matter.

a6047.speaker: US Embassy in Maseru
a6047.speech: Maintained its stance that it has been barred from addressing media enquiries.

a6047.speaker: Mokhethi Shelile, Lesotho Minister of Trade, Industry and Business Development
a6047.speech: Said there was no prior notice that the scheduled meeting with US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer, intended to discuss reducing the 50 percent tariffs on Lesotho's exports, had been cancelled.

a6047.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a6047.speech: During a recent address to Congress, publicly dismissed Lesotho as “a country nobody has heard of” and announced the cancellation of a USD$8 million (M148 million) aid package aimed at promoting LGBTQ+ rights in the Kingdom.

a6124.speaker: Ambassador Alioune Kebe, Liberia's Ambassador for Youth, Sports, and Development
a6124.speech: “My inspiration comes from my own journey. Growing up in Dakar, I was fortunate to have opportunities that others didn’t. While playing professionally in Belgium, I felt a responsibility to give back by creating pathways for young talent in my home country.”

a6124.speaker: Ambassador Alioune Kebe, Liberia's Ambassador for Youth, Sports, and Development
a6124.speech: Lamented: “While Liberia has produced legends like George Weah, the country has struggled to sustain its success in sports. Through this academy, we aim to change that by providing young athletes with the resources, training, and discipline they need to excel.”

a6124.speaker: Ambassador Alioune Kebe, Liberia's Ambassador for Youth, Sports, and Development
a6124.speech: Emphasized: “Discipline is just as important as skill development. We are building a foundation where young athletes grow not just as players, but as disciplined individuals ready to represent Liberia on a global stage.” ; “Liberian talent is undeniable, but we must provide the support and resources to help them succeed.”

a6124.speaker: Ambassador Alioune Kebe, Liberia's Ambassador for Youth, Sports, and Development
a6124.speech: Concluded with an appeal to parents and communities: “Support these initiatives. Together, we can create a future where Liberian sports talent is recognized and celebrated worldwide.”

a6124.speaker: Anthony, a right-back at the Liberia Sports Academy
a6124.speech: “I joined this academy to improve my game and, hopefully, advance to the next level. I encourage Liberians to support their fellow citizens in football. There are so many talented kids out there who just need a chance.”

a6124.speaker: Pastor Annie C. Ihedioha, parent of an academy beneficiary
a6124.speech: “I see this as a great opportunity for our children. My son always dreamed of playing football, and now he has a chance to pursue his passion.” ; “Sports can transform lives, not just financially but through discipline and global exposure. I pray my son achieves his dream, and I believe Liberia will one day be known internationally for its sports talents.” ; “Weah’s achievements were extraordinary, and I hope our children can go even further, putting Liberia’s name on the map.”

a6213.speaker: Abdulla Momade, Chief Representative – SADC at the Dubai Chamber
a6213.speech: Conveyed his elation: “We take immense pride in Aguas da Namaacha being bestowed with the Emirates Quality Mark in Dubai. This prestigious recognition underscores our unwavering commitment to excellence, quality, and the highest industry standards in the beverage sector. Dubai solidifies its position as a top destination for global beverage brands and distinctive offerings worldwide.”

a6213.speaker: Pedro Santos, Director of Exports of the Água da Namaacha company
a6213.speech: “Our entry into the Dubai market has been a colossal undertaking, a testament to the unrelenting efforts of a team of ardent visionaries who believed that achieving the seemingly impossible was indeed possible. I must emphasize that this feat wouldn’t have materialized without the unwavering support of our equally dedicated partner, the Dubai Chambers.”

a6241.speaker: Embassy of the State of Eritrea, Washington, DC (statement)
a6241.speech: Argued that Michael Rubin, whose warmongering commentary has repeatedly championed disastrous interventions in Iraq, Libya and Syria, has a career that is a testament to failed predictions and reckless advocacy, and that his obsession with Eritrea reeks of desperation for relevance; stated that Eritrea built its governance and economy from scratch and has achieved significant progress in healthcare, education and infrastructure; that Eritrea has been a pivotal player in counterterrorism efforts, including collaboration with and training of Somali military forces, and was among the first nations to confront Al-Qaeda in the 1990s; that detractors frequently misrepresent its policy of self-reliance as isolationism while it is some western countries that intermittently attempt to isolate Eritrea; that the national service programme was established to safeguard national security and uphold sovereignty and that mischaracterising it as forced labor disregards its purpose and historical context; that calls for “regime change” reflect a failure to understand the disastrous consequences of similar interventions in Libya and Iraq, and that external interference violates international norms of non-interference; and that what Eritrea seeks is constructive engagement based on mutual respect and understanding, not biased narratives or unjustified criticism.

a6241.speaker: Michael Rubin, US commentator
a6241.speech: Advocates “regime change” in Eritrea and, in his latest piece, “Eritrea Is the North Korea of Africa: America Must Act,” makes critiques the Embassy says exemplify a pattern of misrepresentation and biased narratives.

a6423.speaker: Gemechis Melaku, executive director of export trade at the Ministry of Trade & Regional Integration
a6423.speech: "Buyers are willing to pay premium prices... Sellers tend to ask for more." ; "This practice is exacerbating imported inflation."

a6423.speaker: Ethiopian officials
a6423.speech: Officials hope the new rules will help reverse declining foreign exchange income from oilseeds exports.

a6423.speaker: Atlaw Alemu (PhD), economist lecturing at Addis Abeba University
a6423.speech: Believes the government should have no business intervening in the market; he argued that low productivity and the associated supply shortages drive domestic prices for agricultural commodities. "Rather than controlling prices, it should work on the root causes of the price disparities."

a6423.speaker: The authorities / trade officials
a6423.speech: Remain adamant that the surging prices result from illicit trade and hoarding practices; trade officials claimed to have discovered 60,000tn of cash crops stashed at warehouses owned by 105 exporters following investigations conducted three months ago in Addis Abeba and Adama.

a6423.speaker: Bereket Meseret, trading operations manager for the Ethiopian Commodity Exchange (ECX)
a6423.speech: "The threshold is a tool to prevent the hoarding of commodities anticipating higher prices in the future."

a6423.speaker: Sisay Asmare, president of the Ethiopian Pulses, Oil Seeds & Spices Processors & Exporters Association
a6423.speech: Says the price disparities have been causing frustration among exporters. "The discrepancy in price between the ECX and the international market has meant that exporters are often selling at a loss."

a6423.speaker: Ali Munir, export manager of Munir Hassen Plc
a6423.speech: "There's a cutthroat competition in sourcing oilseeds from the ECX."

a6423.speaker: Capital Atmoisa, chief executive officer of Oliva Agro-Industry Plc
a6423.speech: Exporting sesame may have yielded a high profit in the past; the reverse is true now, according to him; his company faced chronic supply shortages, particularly of oilseeds such as sesame. "We're waiting for the next harvesting season to buy oilseeds." ; "It's been three months since we bought sesame from the trading floor."

a6501.speaker: Government of Burundi
a6501.speech: Praised the unwavering support of the United States of America and that of the ICRC for Burundi.

a6501.speaker: Moïse Nkurunziza, spokesperson for the Prime Minister of Burundi
a6501.speech: Said their discussions focused on strengthening the long-standing ties of friendship and cooperation between Burundi and the United States: “Despite the suspension of certain activities that went through USAID (the American agency for development), the United States of America has shown its full willingness to continue supporting Burundi, especially in the health sector (HIV/AIDS, mother and child nutrition and malaria)” ; reported that the American diplomat specified there is an envelope of 50 million US dollars intended for this sector ; “The Prime Minister welcomed this good gesture of keeping an eye on Burundi” ; “The two figures concluded the discussions with a mutual agreement to continue talking in the interest of our two peoples.”

a6501.speaker: Lisa Peterson, United States Ambassador to Burundi
a6501.speech: Briefly mentioned some of her country’s achievements in terms of support for Burundi and specified that there is an envelope of 50 million US dollars intended for the health sector, indicating that despite the suspension of certain activities that went through USAID the United States has the full willingness to continue supporting Burundi, especially in health (HIV/AIDS, mother and child nutrition and malaria).

a6501.speaker: Nestor Ntahontuye, Prime Minister of Burundi
a6501.speech: Praised the ties of friendship and cooperation between Burundi and the United States of America and welcomed the gesture of “keeping an eye on Burundi”; set out for the American diplomat the administrative and macroeconomic reforms and the rationalisation of the programme budget, all of which falls within the framework of responding to the needs of the population.

a6501.speaker: Kedir Awol Omar, head of the ICRC regional delegation for Burundi, Uganda and Rwanda
a6501.speech: Went over the support that the ICRC continues to provide to the Burundi Red Cross to meet humanitarian needs; spoke of capacity building for members of the defence and security forces so that they carry out their activities in respect of international humanitarian law; mentioned certain actions carried out in the refugee camps in Burundi and thanked Burundi for the welcome and hospitality given to refugees, including those from the DRC.

a6501.speaker: Nestor Ntahontuye, Prime Minister of Burundi
a6501.speech: Praised the ICRC’s efforts and achievements in Burundi, especially its substantial support, and thanked the ICRC for its charitable acts towards humanity not only in Burundi but also in the region.

a6512.speaker: Douglas Rasbash, writer/commentator
a6512.speech: Writes that Botswana needs a new governance architecture based on functionality, synergy, systems thinking and, importantly, one organised to deliver a new style of thematic National Development Plans; that with only 2.7 million people, having 18 ministries and many other MDAs is “government overkill,” and the changes made by the incoming new government are “at best superficial”; that Botswana's ministerial structure, inherited largely from colonial administrative models, has grown fragmented with overlapping mandates, institutional silos and insufficient integration of cross-cutting priorities; and proposes, using a Botswana Governance Synergy Matrix scoring 24 government MDA functions, a reconfiguration into five functionally coherent “super ministries” or Departments of State, implemented cluster by cluster in a phased rollout from January 2026 to December 2028 with a dedicated Reform Implementation Unit — “not another bureaucratic reshuffle but a bold and necessary leap towards a smarter Second Republic.”

a6536.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a6536.speech: In a meeting with Madam Virginia Palmer, the United States Ambassador to Ghana, raised the possibility of renegotiating the abrogated Millennium Challenge Compact, which is intended to inject substantial financial resources into improving the efficiency of Ghana’s energy sector.

a6536.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a6536.speech: At an engagement with captains of industry and business leaders, outlined the modalities of his proposed 10-point, 120-day Social Contract, including swift nomination of Cabinet Ministers for Parliamentary vetting within the first 14 days, establishment of a lean and efficient government by day 90, implementation of a robust code of conduct and standards for all government officials, initiation of a national dialogue focused on fiscal consolidation, operationalizing the Operation Recover All Loot (ORAL) anti-corruption policy, setting up a probe into the National Cathedral project and COVID-19 fund disbursement, and abolishing several levies such as the E-Levy, COVID-19 Levy, 10% betting levy, and emissions levy.

a6536.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a6536.speech: During a courtesy call from the Apostolic Fathers, expressed his intention to soon inaugurate a committee focused on achieving these goals, emphasising: “We have carefully selected the things that we thought were achievable in 120 days. So we are going to work diligently to ensure that at the end of the 120 days, we can check each of them off.”

a6536.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a6536.speech: Cautioned against political opportunism and advised those lobbying for political appointments to deeply reflect on their motivations: “Political appointments are not opportunities for personal gain or power, but rather for real service to the Ghanaian people. Leadership involves sacrifice, humility, and hard work. If you are not prepared to serve diligently and selflessly, do not come. Ghana needs leaders who prioritize the country’s interests over personal ambition.” ; Citing a Ghanaian proverb, reminded potential officeholders: “The cane that was used in beating Baah is the same cane reserved for similar punishment for Takyi.”

a6572.speaker: Mills, U.S. Ambassador to Nigeria (opinion piece)
a6572.speech: Wrote that every December three international observances - World AIDS Day, International Anti-Corruption Day and Human Rights Day - are at the heart of the U.S.-Nigeria partnership and underscore a simple truth, that "Nigeria's path forward requires progress on health, good governance and human rights," adding that "the United States remains your steadfast partner on this journey."

a6572.speaker: Mills, U.S. Ambassador to Nigeria (opinion piece)
a6572.speech: Said that for two decades the United States has stood with Nigeria in the fight against HIV/AIDS under PEPFAR, having invested more than $8.3 billion in Nigeria's health sector and provided life-saving anti-retroviral treatment to more than 1.5 million people, representing improved life expectancy and quality of life for those Nigerians and their families ; said that in clinics across Nigeria he has met dedicated healthcare workers who deliver HIV prevention, treatment and care, supported by the resources of the American people, and that as Nigeria's health system is strengthened this important work will be led by government and engagement with the private sector to sustain the gains.

a6572.speaker: Ambassador Nkengasong
a6572.speech: Held discussions with Nigerian health officials during his recent visit that focused on how the Government of Nigeria would sustain the HIV health programs with strengthened Nigerian leadership and local ownership.

a6572.speaker: Mills, U.S. Ambassador to Nigeria (opinion piece)
a6572.speech: Said positive health outcomes depend critically on good governance, because "when medical supplies are diverted, when healthcare workers go unpaid, when facilities buy dangerous, counterfeit medications or lack resources due to mismanaged funds, it costs lives," which is why the United States supports numerous initiatives to enhance transparency and accountability in Nigeria, working directly with government agencies and civil society organizations to strengthen fiscal responsibility.

a6572.speaker: Mills, U.S. Ambassador to Nigeria (opinion piece)
a6572.speech: Said the success of these efforts rests on respect for human rights and civic engagement, that development falters when marginalized communities face discrimination in accessing healthcare, when citizens fear reporting blatant corruption, or when vulnerable populations cannot advocate for their needs, and that through the partnership with Nigeria the United States promotes the rights of every person to access essential services and enjoy fundamental freedoms without fear or discrimination.

a6572.speaker: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (recent survey)
a6572.speech: Found that Nigerians are both more frequently refusing to pay bribes and reporting bribe seekers to investigative journalists and rule of law authorities.

a6572.speaker: Mills, U.S. Ambassador to Nigeria (opinion piece)
a6572.speech: Said U.S.-supported initiatives have helped strengthen pharmaceutical supply chains, reducing theft and ensuring safe medicines reach patients, that U.S. human rights programming has empowered civil society organizations to advocate for marginalized communities, and that U.S. health system investments have created platforms for transparency that benefit all sectors ; said the U.S. Embassy "stands ready to support Nigerian voices pressing the fight against corruption in Nigeria," told Nigeria's government officials, civil society leaders, healthcare workers and citizens that "your dedication to building a stronger nation inspires us," and said the United States continues to stand with the Nigerian people as they carry out this essential work with their elected government.

a6863.speaker: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS)
a6863.speech: Said on Friday that American budget cuts in aid to foreign countries are sowing “a great deal of disorder” on the ground, despite the waiver granted to programmes fighting the disease.

a6863.speaker: Christine Stegling, Deputy Executive Director of UNAIDS
a6863.speech: “There is a great deal of disorder, particularly at the community level. Community distribution of medicines, transport services, community health workers — all of these services currently remain affected,” she said at a press briefing in Geneva ; while welcoming the PEPFAR waiver, she stressed that the situation remained chaotic ; “In Ethiopia, we count 5,000 contracts of public health workers funded by American aid. All of those contracts have been terminated.”

a6924.speaker: UBA-AGF partnership agreement
a6924.speech: As spelled out in the agreement, the AGF will support and guarantee SMEs with a $50 million portfolio guarantee as well as facilitate extensive capacity development for the bank's burgeoning customers who operate small businesses across the continent, with specific emphasis on women-led businesses and green finance projects.

a6924.speaker: Oliver Alawuba, UBA's Group Managing Director
a6924.speech: Assured that as Africa's Global Bank, UBA remains steadfast in assisting SMEs in Africa where the bank has an operational presence, especially small and medium enterprises managed by women, by virtue of the bank's encompassing network spread across the 20 countries in Africa and major global financial capitals: "This guarantee will catalyse the bank's intervention for SME businesses, women-led and environment-friendly businesses, enabling us to further extend our reach and impact. Additionally, the extensive capacity development initiatives planned for our SME customers across 20 African countries align with our vision to empower businesses, drive innovation, and foster sustainable growth."

a6924.speaker: Oliver Alawuba, UBA's Group Managing Director
a6924.speech: "I am particularly excited about our focus on advancing the AfCFTA initiative, reaffirming UBA's $6 billion commitment to SMEs across Africa. This initiative, announced in September last year, demonstrates our dedication to supporting the economic integration of our continent."

a6924.speaker: Oliver Alawuba, UBA's Group Managing Director
a6924.speech: "Moreover, our commitment to promoting gender equality in our business is reflected in our collaboration with the Affirmative Finance Action for Women (AFAWA) protocol. Through this, we will provide loans to women-owned SMEs at more concessional rates, with customer-friendly collateral terms, aiming to bridge the significant financing gap faced by women in Africa, amounting to $42 billion."

a6924.speaker: Jules Ngankam, Group CEO of the African Guarantee Fund
a6924.speech: Noted that the partnership between the two pan-African institutions, both at the forefront of catalysing growth and development of SMEs, will significantly drive economic growth across the continent: "Small and medium enterprises, despite being the backbone of all African economies, which account for 90% of the private sector and 60% of all jobs, are perceived as risky and therefore have limited access to financing. Through this guarantee facility and the technical capacity development grant support, we will de-risk SMEs, with a priority given to those that are owned or led by women and those that are within the green sector" ; "This partnership is the sequel to the announcement made by United Bank for Africa (UBA) Plc, and the Africa Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat in September 2024, which will help the Bank drive its $6Bn commitment to SMEs across Africa under the AfCFTA initiative."

a6995.speaker: Jafar Haniu, District Commissioner of Rungwe, Mbeya Region
a6995.speech: Directed chief medical officers of the regional hospitals of Mbeya, Songwe, Katavi and Rukwa to supervise the handling and transport of laboratory samples and to strengthen HIV interventions at service-delivery facilities, together with visits to inspect health centres and dispensaries renovated with PEPFAR funding to check whether they match the value of the money spent, and to take action against anyone found to have misappropriated funds ; “Chief medical officers, supervise all the hospitals that benefit through HJFMRI in implementing HIV interventions, including the employment of health-cadre staff, with the aim of carrying out the fight against AIDS, along with the inspection of health centres and dispensaries” ; said the Government will continue to implement AIDS interventions by strengthening laboratory services in hospitals, health centres and dispensaries in collaboration with stakeholders.

a6995.speaker: Dr Sally Chalamila, Director General of HJFMRI Tanzania
a6995.speech: Said the aim of providing the equipment and laboratory machines is to enable service providers to test samples and obtain treatment for patients ; said the laboratories will improve the availability of services in those regions, with the aim of bringing services to the community.

a6995.speaker: Mark Breda, resident director of WRAIR
a6995.speech: Said they will continue to collaborate with the Government of Tanzania in the fight against new HIV infections ; “This equipment, worth Sh132.9 million, has been provided to the regions of Mbeya, Songwe, Rukwa and Katavi, along with a cervical cancer screening machine worth Sh30 million.”

a6995.speaker: Dr Jonathan Ludemo, Katavi Regional Medical Officer
a6995.speech: Said the laboratory equipment will bring benefits to Tanzanians and enable them to receive appropriate services ; “On behalf of my colleagues from the southern highlands regions, we have seen how stakeholders are improving the availability of services for testing samples of various diseases in bringing services to the community.”

a7010.speaker: European Commission (statement)
a7010.speech: "The European Commission has committed to granting a further 40 million euros of humanitarian aid to the Democratic Republic of Congo, subject to approval by the budgetary authority. [...] The EU had already promised 60 million euros for the country in January 2025 and today's pledge raises total aid to 100 million euros in 2025."

a7010.speaker: Hadja Lahbib, European Commissioner for Preparedness and Crisis Management
a7010.speech: Declared, in a statement, that the crisis in the DR Congo "is a humanitarian catastrophe" that leaves more than 20 million people in need of humanitarian aid and more than seven million people internally displaced ; "The suffering is immense and I convened this ministerial round table as a call to action: we have to turn words into aid, commitments into relief and solidarity into lasting solutions" ; concluded that "the world cannot stand idly by" without providing aid.

a7010.speaker: European Parliament / MEPs (resolution)
a7010.speech: Condemned the "serious human rights violations" committed in the DR Congo by rebel forces, calling for a ceasefire; in a show-of-hands vote, MEPs denounced the "alarming continuation of the violence" caused by the advance of the rebels of the March 23 Movement (M23) and of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) and demanded the withdrawal of Rwandan forces in the country; the approved text also called for an immediate ceasefire in the eastern region of the DR Congo.

a7324.speaker: Mamadou Lamine Bah, retired divisional police commissioner
a7324.speech: "Indeed, the use of slate roofing dates back, according to the accounts, to just after the Second World War. It was a Frenchman who detected this slate deposit at Thialakoun and who put it to use. So it was used to cover many administrative buildings, the main ones being the prefecture, the post office, the social housing, and also within the grounds of the Public Works department, where the buildings in question are being razed. The civil prison was also covered with slate, and in some towns of Guinea too, because I remember that in Kankan there was a building that was also covered with slate."

a7324.speaker: Mamadou Lamine Bah, retired divisional police commissioner
a7324.speech: Calls for the State to intervene to save what remains of this built heritage: "What must be remembered is that Labe had this cachet of having many houses covered with slate. So we must really ensure that this cachet is maintained... those who were trained in the practice of this roofing have practically all passed away... It is the administration that should see to it that outside expertise is called upon, if only to restore the buildings or maintain the slate roofs. In any case, these roofs are not only original and aesthetic, but above all they are solid, soundproof and keep the house cool. Moreover, if the activity is resumed, it will lower the cost price of a roof, since the quarry is there, open to the sky, a stone's throw from the town, and the State will gain, as will the citizens. In addition, it will make it possible to train qualified workers and reduce youth unemployment. And why not, this new expertise could even be exported elsewhere" ; "these are historic buildings that must be preserved; even if it is private, the State must seek to maintain them. Take the example of the Vatican... The Kremlin, it is the same thing; the White House had been burned after the war of independence by the English who had seized Washington. But it was reconstituted. Here, we have lost that culture; so this is an opportunity for the ministry of culture to take this up, in order to preserve historic built heritage."

a7324.speaker: Elhadj Mamadou Diallo, elder encountered in the administrative district of Labe
a7324.speech: Considers it very regrettable: "Imagine, from the colonial period to the present day, that is to say a little more than 70 years, buildings such as the prefecture and the post office, to name only those two, are still standing with a roof that does not go unnoticed. That should make us think and push us to exploit this important slate deposit that God has given us. But instead of that we are progressively demolishing the buildings covered in slate in order to build apartment blocks. A shame for us."

a7324.speaker: Ibrahima Sory Sidibe, regional inspector of mines and geology
a7324.speech: "The houses covered with slate are very pretty to see in Labe, it is just that there is no progress with this kind of roofing, whereas less than three kilometres from the town centre we have an important deposit of quality slate."

a7382.speaker: Qatar and the United States (joint announcement)
a7382.speech: Announced an agreement providing for a ceasefire in Gaza and the release of hostages, marking a key step after more than 15 months of deadly conflict between Israel and Hamas.

a7382.speaker: Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Prime Minister of Qatar
a7382.speech: Said the agreement comprises a three-phase ceasefire; the first phase, scheduled to begin on 19 January, would last six weeks and include a withdrawal of Israeli troops from densely populated areas and the release of 33 hostages, including women and children, with Israel in return freeing hundreds of Palestinian prisoners.

a7382.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a7382.speech: Hailed a "full ceasefire," while mentioning a monitoring mechanism led by Egypt, Qatar and the United States.

a7382.speaker: Bezalel Smotrich, Israeli Finance Minister
a7382.speech: Denounced a "dangerous agreement," reflecting divisions within the Israeli government.

a7382.speaker: United Nations (casualty figures)
a7382.speech: Deemed reliable the figures of 1,210 deaths on the Israeli side and more than 46,700 victims in the Gaza Strip since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023.

a7382.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a7382.speech: Stresses the importance of lifting the obstacles to humanitarian aid.

a7387.speaker: Christine Marchand-Pardo, Delta's Managing Director of EMEAI Operations
a7387.speech: "Delta's new nonstop service to Marrakech marks an exciting milestone in our commitment to connect the U.S. and Africa. This route opens the door to one of the world's most vibrant and culturally rich destinations, making travel more seamless for our customers. With three weekly flights from Atlanta, we're delivering convenience alongside Delta's renowned premium experience. From lie-flat seats in Delta One to curated dining and thoughtful amenities across all cabin experiences, customers can expect comfort at every step of their journey. This expansion also reinforces Atlanta's position as the world's leading global hub, offering convenient one-stop connectivity, while bringing the magic of Marrakech closer than ever."

a7387.speaker: Delta Air Lines (press release distributed by African Media Agency)
a7387.speech: Announced it has officially launched its first nonstop flight between Atlanta (ATL) and Marrakech (RAK), becoming the first U.S. airline to operate the route, with three-times-a-week service initially and daily service between December 18 and January 6, 2026; stated that since launching its first African service in 2006 Delta has flown over 7.5 million passengers to the continent, now serves six African cities, and operates nearly 1,000 daily flights to 215 destinations worldwide from its Atlanta hub.
